findings.claim: On a clean or aborted stream close, `done === true` is now turned into a thrown generic `Error('Stream closed unexpectedly')`, which can fire during normal teardown (client abort / server closing the stream) and surface as a noisy error rather than a cancellation.
findings.rationale: `read()` also returns `done: true` when the stream is closed deliberately (abort/cancel of the consumer). The new branch makes no distinction between abnormal truncation and an intentional close, so previously-silent teardown paths may now reject. Confidence: medium — depends on whether the controller/reader is closed on abort, which isn't visible in this hunk.

findings.claim: The thrown error is a plain `Error` with no `cause` or chunk context and is not a `TRPCError`, changing the rejection type callers previously observed (a `TypeError` from destructuring `undefined`).
findings.rationale: Elsewhere in tRPC stream code errors are typically wrapped in `TRPCError` so they map to a proper error shape/code; a bare `Error` may bypass error-formatting expectations, and existing callers catching/inspecting the old TypeError would behave differently. Including the pending chunk id would also make truncated-stream debugging feasible. Confidence: medium.

findings.claim: Rejecting inside `run(async () => ...)` can produce an unhandled promise rejection if the deserialized promise for this chunk is never awaited by the consumer.
findings.rationale: The returned promise is handed to user code; if the stream truncates while the user never awaits that particular nested promise, the new throw becomes an unhandled rejection (process crash under `--unhandled-rejections=throw`). The pre-existing destructuring TypeError had the same hazard, but this change makes the truncation path an explicit and more commonly hit rejection. Consider routing through the existing deferred/error handling. Confidence: low-to-medium.
